scenes.title: Wavelength: compute at carrier edge
scenes.visual_overview: The original slide explains wavelength: compute at carrier edge using 4 explicitly labelled visual sections, connections, and practical limits.
visual_walkthrough: Deploy supported compute near mobile users on carrier infrastructure
Create a Wavelength Zone subnet as an extension of the parent Region VPC
Use a carrier gateway and appropriate carrier addressing and routes
Validate available capacity, carrier reach, regional dependencies, supported inbound path and security
scenes.visual_example: A mobile streaming backend uses Wavelength to reduce latency but must test the carrier path and service availability in the selected zone.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Validate the wavelength: compute at carrier edge design with supported network settings, complete traffic paths and its actual failure domains.
scenes.narration: This lesson explains wavelength: compute at carrier edge, using the actual architecture and numbered callouts on the screen. Start with the first element: Deploy supported compute near mobile users on carrier infrastructure. Notice the depicted connections and boundaries; they illustrate which component owns this responsibility. Next, follow the second section: Create a Wavelength Zone subnet as an extension of the parent Region VPC. This changes how the path or control is configured, and should be checked rather than assumed. Move to the third section: Use a carrier gateway and appropriate carrier addressing and routes. For a working design, distinguish a successful control-plane configuration from application-level reachability, security and service readiness. Now inspect the final section: Validate available capacity, carrier reach, regional dependencies, supported inbound path and security. Consider a realistic architecture scenario. A mobile streaming backend uses Wavelength to reduce latency but must test the carrier path and service availability in the selected zone. When troubleshooting, test the forward and return paths, the relevant service-specific limits and actual user traffic, then compare the result with the requirement. The key takeaway is to select the correct model and prove its behaviour under normal operation and failure.
